subject: Business Models
title: Globalization and Outsourcing
description: A micro-lesson that makes Globalization and Outsourcing usable.

hook.text: A typical iPhone is designed in California, assembled in China, with parts from 43 countries.

buildup.text: Globalization lets companies optimize every step: cheapest labor, best materials, fastest shipping.

discovery.text: Container shipping made this possible. A 40-foot box costs $2,000 to send across the Pacific.

twist.text: COVID revealed the fragility. When one factory in China closes, car plants in Germany stop.

climax.text: Companies now balance efficiency with resilience. 'Just in time' shifts to 'just in case.'

punchline.text: 43 countries in your pocket. Globalization built that phone.

quiz.question: What revolution enabled modern global supply chains?

details.summary: Late 20th century globalization enabled companies to fragment production across countries, outsourcing manufacturing to low-wage economies while retaining design, marketing, and management in developed nations..
details.whyItMatters: Globalization reshuffled the world economy, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty in developing nations while displacing manufacturing workers in developed countries..
takeaways: Companies fragment production across countries to optimize labor and material costs
Container shipping and trade agreements made global supply chains economically viable
Outsourcing generated savings for companies while displacing workers in developed nations

faq.question: What enabled the globalization of production in the late 20th century?
faq.answer: Container shipping cut transport costs 90 percent. Trade agreements like NAFTA and WTO rules reduced tariffs. Digital communication enabled coordination across time zones. Financial deregulation allowed capital to flow to lowest-cost production locations..

faq.question: Is globalization reversing due to reshoring trends?
faq.answer: Partially. COVID exposed supply chain fragility. Geopolitical tensions, especially with China, are driving reshoring and friend-shoring efforts. Rising wages in developing nations narrow cost advantages. Automation makes domestic production more competitive..
